listeningScripts.title: Arranging a Broadband Installation
listeningScripts.text:
Advisor: Good morning, Kestrel Broadband, Priya speaking.
Caller: Hello, I've just moved and I need to arrange an installation.
Advisor: I can help with that. Can I take your name?
Caller: It's Marcus Vandeleur. That's V-A-N-D-E-L-E-U-R.
Advisor: And the installation address?
Caller: Fourteen Sandpiper Close.
Advisor: Let me check what's available there. You can have the standard fibre package, which is sixty megabits, or the faster one at five hundred.
Caller: What's the difference in price?
Advisor: The standard is twenty-nine pounds a month and the faster is forty-four. Can I ask what you use it for?
Caller: Working from home, mostly video calls.
Advisor: Then the standard is genuinely enough. Video calls need very little, and people upgrade for it far more often than they need to.
Caller: I'll take the standard, then.
Advisor: Sensible. Now, is there an existing socket in the property?
Caller: There's one in the hallway, but I want the router in the back room.
Advisor: That's fine — the engineer can move it, but it adds about forty minutes, so I'll book a longer slot. There's no charge for that.
Caller: Good. When can you come?
Advisor: The earliest is Tuesday the eleventh of March, morning, which is eight until one.
Caller: I can't do mornings. What about afternoons?
Advisor: The afternoon slot is one until six, and the next available is Thursday the thirteenth.
Caller: Thursday afternoon, please.
Advisor: Booked. Someone over eighteen must be at the property for the whole slot — the engineer can't be left alone in the house.
Caller: Understood. Is there an installation fee?
Advisor: Normally thirty-five pounds, but it's waived on a twelve-month contract, which is what I've put you on.
Caller: And how long does it take?
Advisor: About ninety minutes, or a little over two hours with the socket move. Your equipment arrives separately, two days before — don't open it until the engineer's there.

listeningScripts.title: City Farm Volunteer Briefing
listeningScripts.text:
Coordinator: Morning, everybody, and thank you for coming to volunteer at Marsh Lane City Farm. I'm Owen, and I run the volunteer programme.

I want to start with the animals, because that's what most people come for and it's where I have to manage expectations. Volunteers do not handle the animals in the first three months. You'll be mucking out, filling water, moving feed and cleaning equipment. Handling requires knowing how each animal behaves when it's frightened, and that takes a season of watching before it takes any training.

Sessions are Tuesday to Sunday, and we ask for one four-hour session a week. If you can't come, please tell us — the animals get fed either way, which means somebody else does your work, and knowing on Friday is very different from finding out on Sunday morning.

Clothing: sturdy boots, and clothes you will not mind ruining. Not wellingtons, which are cold and slip on the concrete when it's wet. We provide gloves.

Let me point out the layout, since the site is confusing. Coming through the gate, the volunteer hut is straight in front of you — that's where you sign in and leave bags. The goat and sheep paddocks are on the left, running along the western fence. The poultry area is at the far northern end, past the paddocks, deliberately away from the entrance because the birds are the most easily startled by visitors. Opposite the paddocks, on the eastern side, are the raised vegetable beds, and the polytunnel is behind them in the north-eastern corner. The feed store is beside the volunteer hut, on its right as you face it.

Two rules that matter. Gates: every gate is closed behind you, every time, even if you are coming straight back through it in ten seconds. And handwashing before you eat or drink anything, without exception — this is a farm, and that rule is the reason we have never had an incident.

listeningScripts.title: Designing a Questionnaire
listeningScripts.text:
Tutor: Right — the questionnaire for your study on cycling. Let me see the draft. Question one: "Don't you agree that the new cycle lanes have improved safety?"
Elena: Is that not clear?
Tutor: It's perfectly clear. It also tells the respondent what you want them to say. "Don't you agree" invites agreement, and "improved" assumes the thing you're asking about.
Elena: So how would I ask it?
Tutor: Neutrally. "How has your sense of safety changed since the cycle lanes were installed?" with a scale from much worse to much better, and the middle option available.
Tom: What about question four — "How often do you cycle?" with options: never, sometimes, often.
Tutor: What does "often" mean?
Tom: I suppose it depends on the person.
Tutor: Exactly, and that means you cannot compare two answers. Ask for a count in a defined period: "On how many days in the last seven did you cycle?" That is answerable and comparable.
Elena: This one asks about age and income at the start.
Tutor: Move those to the end. People are more willing to give personal details once they have invested effort, and putting them first is the commonest reason a questionnaire is abandoned at question two.
Tom: How long should the whole thing be?
Tutor: Time it yourself, then assume respondents will take half as long as you think they should and give up at ten minutes. Aim for under eight.
Elena: Do we need to pilot it?
Tutor: Yes, on about ten people, and not on each other — you both know what the questions mean, which is precisely what a pilot is testing. Sit with them and watch where they hesitate. The hesitation tells you more than their answers do.

listeningScripts.title: Why Buildings Overheat
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: Buildings in temperate countries were designed for a problem that is becoming less pressing and against a problem that is becoming more so. They were built to retain heat, and they now overheat, and I want to look at why the fix is harder than adding air conditioning.

The first thing to understand is where the heat comes from. In a well-insulated modern building, the largest summer heat input is usually not the outside air temperature but solar gain through glazing — sunlight entering through windows and being absorbed inside. A room with substantial south or west-facing glass can gain more heat in an afternoon than its occupants and equipment produce all day.

That points at the most effective intervention, which is shading, and specifically shading on the outside. A blind inside the glass stops the light after it has already entered and become heat; a shutter, overhang or external blind stops it before. The difference between the two is large — external shading can cut solar gain by most of its value, internal shading by a fraction of it — and internal blinds are what almost everyone installs, because they are cheap, adjustable and do not require touching the outside of the building.

Insulation cuts both ways and is widely misunderstood. It slows heat movement in either direction, so a well-insulated building is slower to warm and also slower to cool once warm. In a climate with hot days and cool nights, that is only useful if the building can be purged of heat overnight — which requires openable windows, secure ventilation, and someone willing to open them.

Which brings us to the constraint that decides most of this. Night ventilation depends on being able to leave windows open, and in many buildings that is prevented by security, by noise, by air quality, or by the windows themselves, which in a large number of recent buildings do not open at all. A design that requires night purging and a building that cannot be opened is a common and expensive combination.

The uncomfortable conclusion is about sequence. Air conditioning works, and installing it in a building that has not been shaded first means running it against a solar gain that could have been removed for a fraction of the energy. Cooling is the last step in a sensible order and is routinely the first step taken, because it is the one that can be bought and fitted without altering anything about the building.
